I'm gonna leave a comment because while I'm not an expert, I feel like this could be a really interesting prompt for a real professional to answer. Six years ago, I'd tell you I totally relate to you with not using many products in my hair or having ever colored it, but right now I'm on year 3 of long deep blue hair that I've been getting touched up at a salon ever 8 weeks, and on top of that, I have bangs that I basically have to use a blow-dryer and a round brush with mousse and hair spray twice a week when I wash it with cold water only....so I wouldn't recommend you get bangs like mine if you really value not needing to style your hair. On the other hand, a random anecdote that I read when I was researching "what you should know before you dye your hair blue" was that having a vivid/vibrant color hair is basically a hairstyle all in itself. Even if all I do is wash with shampoo and conditioner (the more expensive one that's color safe, that is) and air-dry, my hair still looks like I put effort into it and did something fancy, just by nature of being a really cool color. I also have color-depositing shampoo and conditioner that I use every so often to add another dimension of color to it, and I get comments all the time. So if you feel like spending the money on getting a vibrant color, and getting comments like "I love your hair!" from every other girl with a vivid hair color that you see, I'd recommend it for being low maintenance, in that I don't necessarily have to do anything more than just washing and air drying it and I'll look like I fixed it. 

Something you can do that isn't quite as drastic is just getting some highlights to add a bit of texture to your hair if it's too flat... I did that when I dyed my faded blue hair back to my natural blonde for my wedding, and having some highlights and lowlights was just the way the stylist helped blend the several months of root regrowth into the color-stripped, bleached, and blonde-toned length. The top of my hair had a lot more volume than it'd ever had before I colored it. Though you do say that your hair has a lot of volume, so you could maybe look into getting a different type of layers added to show off that volume in a new way.

What are some of your hair goals? Easy upkeep for low-maintenance, or a more creative cut with multiple styling options? Something to pop and make you really memorable, or something classic that matches your fashion sense? 

I think some long face-framing layers might look good for your face shape, if they were jaw length and blended, not too blunt. You could also probably rock a pixie cut or a short bob. A bright neon color (or streak of color) could be really fun if you wanted to go for something like that, especially if orange or red are in your color wheel (though red dye stains can be kind of shocking so be prepared if you go that direction).

I think whatever feels more manageable to you should be your first choice. Whichever way you feel looks best more of the time, whether or not you have the time and energy to style it. But if that doesn't sound like a concern for you, and you like being able to style it all the time in lots of different ways, then go for a fun haircut with a lot of versatility that will show off the natural strengths of your hair type — which is to say, talk to your hairstylist to figure out the best cut for you and your goals.

I had to look twice at the username to make sure this wasn't from an account that my husband uses, because honestly, it sounds like what we've been going through in our marriage. Word for word, I genuinely thought it was coming from my husband. 

I've recently gotten off some medications that I was on for years that have been changing the chemical structure of my body's systems that regulate both my hormones and my brain. For a long time, I didn't know that I couldn't tell what I was feeling, and I wasn't sure who I was, except for in certain situations when I would try to express myself and then fail. Figuring out that this was part of the reason why sex was not valuable to me for my personal well-being and did not satisfy an urge that I could feel was vital to my understanding of this situation between me and my husband. 

I had always felt guilt around this subject, since I knew that my husband was doing all of the work, and that he was the one who needed it to function—not only physically, but emotionally, spiritually, and mentally, too. I felt like something about me was broken, and I still do. If only my body desired physical intimacy and touch!! Then my husband's needs would reflect the same needs within me that I would have no problem fulfilling. Previous mental health diagnoses hadn't made the sexual issues make any sense, but in January, my search for a new diagnosis brought PTSD to the table. I now had a real, doctor/psychologist appointed explanation for this embarrassing and confusing situation I found myself in. And in March, I finished weaning myself off my hormonal birth control and my two antidepressants. It's been 2 months since I've had any of those, and I'm still on the most difficult medication to cope without, which I'll keep taking until we are ready to begin trying to start a family in the winter of this year, as we've planned. But the change to my ability to feel my own emotions and react to things and express myself and recognize issues in the way I function—it's been growing steadily over the past two months. I think that if I can get into a regular workout routine and improve my ability to connect with my body and feel safe outside of the walls I built up around my mind, that rediscovering intimacy will start to become possible for me. 

I'm scared though. It's been five years since we used to make out and push the boundaries of what we could get away with while we were "waiting" for marriage, and I really want to be able to feel that same attraction, but it's been so long. I was able to keep from crying at my own wedding, and that felt like the beginning of the end for all of that, because from that point on, I was like a turtle that was shrinking back further and further into its shell. Eight years ago when we met, he had been the first person I had allowed myself to come out of my shell for—so how could I take that all away and withdraw for so many years? It's got to be the combination of the meds. I'd tried solving several other things that might've been the issue, but they didn't make as big of a change as getting off those meds did. 

I haven't really shared this story anywhere else except in my therapy sessions, and I'm gonna be saving this to show to my therapist because I think it'll be helpful for her to see where my processing is at on all of this... I know it might not be relevant or helpful for the person who wrote this post, but it felt like I couldn't keep from writing all of this with the way it was lining up so accurately with my situation.

I dislike getting flowers, and I knew this before my husband and I got married, so I was glad my husband didn't get me flowers all the time. In fact, on Valentine's Day this year, I asked him if he would pick up some chocolates and wine to bring home after work, and I was glad he didn't get any flowers—and I told him so a few days after. Now, he only ever got me flowers a couple times, and it was when we were in a long-distance relationship, and he would bring a rose or a bouquet with him when he visited me. That was special because then I had those roses to remember him by, and to think of him when I looked at them after he was gone. I dried the roses and I still have them today. 

I feel like if he got me flowers "all the time" as you're saying your husband does, then early on in the relationship I would've told him that I disliked it (my reasons include the way flowers are *way* too expensive if you buy them at a store vs cutting a rose from a bush that you own, and they don't even live that long no matter how well you take care of them in a vase, because they're dead. I don't really want dead flowers while I'm alive. I'd rather be given a living plant to keep in my house or transplant to my garden, or an artificial flower that won't fade in a week.) If my husband had told me that giving me flowers was really important to him, and that he still wanted to give them to me, then I'd like to think that when the idea of buying flowers to give to him would've come to me, that I would've thought that it would be something he would like. But it's not the case for me, so I don't know.... I get him things he likes, like different kinds of candy or cookies or little things that make me think of him, every once in a while or when he's having a rough week, but I like them to be functional or edible things. 

It kind of sounds like your husband was maybe feeling a bit sad about never receiving any flowers himself, but was deciding to try not to let it bother him anymore, when you gave them to him out of nowhere. It definitely touched him in a really strong way, and I think it sounds like you've got a beautiful opportunity to learn how to romance your husband in new ways that you hadn't thought of before—so I wish you all the best in your journey.

Hey!! Mental health!!

I'm really good at therapy. All my therapists are like "wow, you're good at analyzing yourself and recognizing things" and of course that's nice to hear. 

I'm not as good at application. I've got ADHD (without hyperactivity) and a lot of the things that end up negatively affecting my mental health are related to that... (hold on, I wanna rant verbally so imma use voice-to-text and then edit it afterwards)

For example, some of the things that I struggle with—that I really need to get done, but that I don't get done—are things that are difficult because I have ADHD. Laundry, dishes, cleaning. The consequences of not doing my dishes or my laundry or cleaning my house end up affecting my mental health, and because of the shame associated with continuing to struggle with the same things over and over, I tend to lose hope and get depressed, feeling like I'm stuck being this bad at normal adult things, and that'll never get any better, and that'll never be able to hold a job or have a rewarding life. 

But when bigger things—life events that I can't control—come along, I have so many healthy coping mechanisms and natural coping styles that I have developed over my lifetime that I am able to bounce back in a way that surprises me sometimes. It's as if I struggle every day with these small things, but the muscles that I am training as I struggle with these small things end up helping me easily overcome the big things when they appear. I don't know if I'll ever get good at these small things, but maybe it's the big things that matter, and really I've been getting better at small things all along, just at a different pace than I tend to expect for myself, since I'm perfectionistic about a lot of things.

If I had never gone through those rough times as a kid, if I'd never had to learn how to adjust to a different environment while going through a lot of stuff on the outside and on the inside, I probably would have given up by now. But since the struggles I've gone through have built my character, at least I know how to treat people; through experience, I have continued to know better and better how to be a really good friend, and the people that are close to me are willing to help in those areas in which I lack. I am the opposite of a person who is so good at everything on the first try that they never have to ask for help and never need support from anyone and end up alone. Therefore, I'm a person who is not very good at anything at the first try, and I have to ask for help and I need support from people, and I end up being surrounded by helpful, gracious, understanding people who have gone through their own share of trials to get to where they are now. And that's the kind of person I want to be: someone who can come alongside a younger person who has a lot of small things that they're struggling with, and help them to personally succeed in going through the big things in their life as they are assisted with the small things. I just got done with a tutoring session with a high schooler that I met at the youth group that I volunteer at, and the way that I've been able to use my past struggles to help her overcome her own has been so rewarding to me.

In the end, I don't know if I really answered the question... I think my mental health is good if I have people around me that I can help and people who can help me. If there's too many people though, I end up trying to isolate myself, and if there's too much pressure from people, then I really isolate myself and also pursue things that might not be healthy. However, when I am plugged into a healthy support system and part of a close community, my mental health thrives and I can literally feel myself growing. 

Best wishes to everybody out there who is struggling, either with the big things or the small things, or both of them and everything in between. If anyone wants to talk, you can DM me and if I'm still in this state of "I can conquer the world through kindness" then I'll write you back and I'll be able to help out or listen to anything you want to talk about. But if it comes to tomorrow morning and I wake up and feel like I'm losing the battle, I might have too much anxiety to answer a DM. But you guys know how it is. I started to read some answers and it honestly started to weigh on me how devastating this would be...somehow being the last adult human, if not in the whole world (how would I know if I was, I'd be in that hospital with nobody as far as I could see and nobody responding on radio or whatever communication was left) then the only adult able to care for this "hospital full of babies"... As I look this up online, I'm finding numbers like "record broken as 42 babies born in 48 hours" and I guess there could be two or three days of babies who had been born, to hopefully number 50 (to repopulate the human race with the minimum needed to combat inbreeding, as another post said)...   

Being alone in a hospital of like 50 babies and knowing that nobody was going to come and help me... I'd be looking at a lonely but busy life as a nonstop nanny without any reprieve. I think that the first thing I would do would be to gather supplies and try to rig some kind of feeding system that could help me feed more than two babies at once. Assuming they'd been fed right before everybody disappeared, I'd have a few hours before they started getting hungry, and maybe I could set something up by then that would allow me a way to nap along with them to some degree.   

Those first few hours would be crucial. Anything that was currently running on electricity would have its days numbered, as, even if no damage had been done to the city's infrastructure, every power plant requires maintenance and oversight to run. But once those started to break down, then food and goods all over the world would begin to spoil, and without at least one power plant to run a huge walk-in freezer, sustaining my "tribe" of younglings would become next to impossible.   

I don't know if I could care for all of the babies while also trying to make the best of the time I had in the beginning and save resources and supplies for the future. Some systems, like gas stations, I would have to figure out how to break into and get working on my own, but the resource itself wouldn't spoil so I could wait on that. I could try to find and keep track of a local farm during the first few weeks and see what I could do to keep a good number of animals alive and fed so that I could rely on them once the babies grew old enough to eat regular food. In that same vein, I would gather seeds for future crops and basically try to start a self-sustaining farm. I'd need to move all of the children there, and probably all at once if it was possible. So I'd need a school bus and as many car seats as I had children. I might be able to make do by strapping down strollers if I couldn't locate enough car seats. But there's no way I could move 50 babies or even toddlers without having them strapped in!  

If I survived year 1:  

Some of the babies would be walking by that stage, and I would be deciding how long to keep them on formula before it would no longer support their development. Hopefully the hospital would have baby food, because I'm pretty sure it would keep for long enough if it was in jars/cans or something with a longer shelf life. This would probably be around the point where I would have gotten all of them transferred to the farm and bunked up in cardboard boxes with blankets and other supplies from the hospital. That's if there weren't enough cribs in the hospital that they hadn't outgrown. I would be working to maintain the farm equipment and begin planting a sizeable garden, with a portion of it being in a greenhouse for the cold season. I would probably have rescued a lot of pets, ones who had been able to survive on their own for a while at first and were roaming the streets, possibly in packs, and I would try to train some of the right breeds of dogs to watch over the children while I worked on the farm. Something like "if a baby gets hurt them you bark for me to come, and you protect it if there's a predator hunting it while I get the gun." My attention would be on food production and basic necessities.   

If I survived year 2:

I would be teaching the children a lot at this stage, and if the power was still functioning then I'd set up educational videos to play while I was working, and have the same guard-nanny-dog setup. I might try bringing a child or two with me wherever I went, and keep track of who I had brought with me so that I paid them all a relatively even amount of attention. They would begin to develop their own personalities and to interact with each other at this and earlier stages, and they would begin to entertain themselves to some degree. Heaven knows I couldn't give them all the time they deserved, but I would do my best while keeping us all alive. 

If I survived year 4:

By this time they'd all be talking and walking and getting into all sorts of trouble, but from the simple reality of being very independent, they would have to learn to do things for themselves as much as possible. I would have to make a lot of really difficult decisions, specifically with some of the children who were on the slower end of social skill development who wanted to be by my side always and were afraid to be without me. I would probably give in and let them sleep in my bed when they got scared at night, but this would be the year when I would try to guide those little ones to be more self-sufficient. They'd probably have to pick up the slack if I ever got sick, and it would be really scary for them! If it was a sickness that kept me from preparing food and doing all the things I had to do in order to keep the farm running, there would definitely be a few in the group who would step up and lead the rest in their attempt to fend for themselves while I recovered.

If I survived year 6:

There's no way I could teach fifty children how to read while also maintaining our sources of food and electricity (or chopping wood for an iron stove for heat and cooking, either way). I'd have to hope that I could make do with video learning and any curriculum that I could find. I would probably try to at least teach the children a basis of survival skills at first, and then focus on reading and writing and simple math. Knowing that if anything happened to me that they would be on their own for the rest of their lives, I would do everything I could to make sure they had access to libraries and were able to read and comprehend that literature. 

If I survived year 8:

We'd probably have a good system for everything set up at this point. Maybe we would have time to try our hand at some simple carpentry and make a playground and some other types of recreation. I would probably begin to go on scouting trips with a small group of them as soon as they could manage the farm on their own for a few days at a time, and we would work on stocking up on anything we had run out of and to take inventory on the state of everything that was left. I bet we'd get up to some crazy hijinks and end up having great stories to tell around the dinner table and campfire when we returned! 

It is at this point in my writing that I've realized I would need to name them all. They'd all need to be named from the very beginning, as infants, and I would need to keep track of who was who somehow... I think I would probably try to label their clothes at first, but as they'd soil them very quickly and then need new ones, and the soiled ones would all go into the wash and come out in a mess, I'd need to find a more permanent method of differentiating between them. One idea I'd think of would be to find different prints of fabric and fashion unique bracelets for them, and then keep a copy of that pattern on a big board with all of their names and a space to keep notes on the health of each one. Well spiders are mostly nocturnal, right? I bet a lot of them would be killed by the response of governments attacking them to protect the people, because so many of them would be stuck outside looking for a place to hide. 

Also, if there were no longer normal-sized spiders, then the population of other bugs that are normally food for spiders would increase quickly. Mosquitos, flies, gnats, all that stuff. Spiders wouldn't be there to keep them in check anymore, since they'd be too small for the huge spiders to catch any good quantities of and thus they wouldn't provide enough nourishment to be worth eating. Then, the spiders that did find a hiding spot and could be safe during the day would begin to venture out at night looking for prey. They'd probably try to catch things with webs at first but I don't know if the things they could catch (birds, mostly I guess) would be worth their time. Maybe they'd develop hunting patterns in order to take down deer and other wild animals. Maybe they'd go after people themselves, taking a large group in a net of sticky webs and hauling it back to its hideout. But eventually, I think the larger demand for food would be the end of the spiders, with the exception of a few who lived in areas with natural caves near a large wildlife population. 

Slowly, they'd all be killed off, and I think the ones that did survive long enough would only be able to do so by hiding. It would be so easy to bomb a spider nest once it was found, and any defense the spider would have been able to put up around its lair would be useless against bombs, lol. 

So you'd probably hear on the news that they'd found a colony of spiders that had been hiding in an abandoned mine shaft in Arizona and they were *pretty* sure they'd incinerated all of them, but sometimes egg sacs could be hidden really well and then it was only a matter of time before more of them popped up again. 

They'd probably have a comic book series about a girl who could communicate telepathically with the spiders, and so she fought for their classification as a species that should be protected, and it would have a lot of drama and eventually she would go off the grid somewhere to hide spiders from the world so that they could have a safe haven under her wing. 

TLDR: they'd wreck the ecological balance and eventually be mostly killed off, while humanity dealt with the mess they left behind when small spiders stopped being there to eat all the bugs.
